registered.new: Drennan protected the general contractor that reasonably used a definite bid in its own bid. Protection fails if the bid expressly or clearly reserved a power to revoke before acceptance, or if the general knew or had reason to know the bid was mistaken. registered.old: Use § 2-207 for qualifying sales. Under common law, a response that makes assent contingent on new conditions may instead be a counteroffer. A mere inquiry can leave acceptance intact.
registered.new: Use § 2-207 for qualifying sales. Dorton requires language that clearly shows the offeree will not proceed without the offeror’s assent; “subject to” its printed terms is not enough.

registered.new: A promise to hold an offer open is enforceable if supported by consideration, made enforceable by statute (UCC § 2-205 or N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1109), or written and signed, reciting a purported consideration and proposing a fair exchange within a reasonable time (Restatement § 87(1)); the Restatement calls this an option contract (§ 25). An offer also becomes irrevocable when it seeks acceptance by performance and the offeree tenders or begins performance (§§ 45, 62), or when it has been relied on (§ 87(2)). Legal qualification: § 2-205 reaches only a merchant’s offer to buy or sell goods in a signed writing that by its terms assures it will be held open, for the stated or a reasonable time but no more than three months, with a separate signature for an assurance on the offeree’s form; § 5-1109 requires a signed writing stating that the offer is irrevocable and yields to § 2-205 for a merchant’s goods offer. Under § 45 beginning performance of an offer that invites only performance creates an option, and the offeror’s duty stays conditional on completion; under § 62 beginning performance of an offer that invites either a promise or performance is an acceptance that binds the offeree to finish. Section 87(2) requires reliance of a substantial character that the offeror should reasonably expect before acceptance, and binds only to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.

Firm offers and the § 2-207 between-merchants rule have distinct requirements: § 2-205 asks only whether the offeror is a merchant, while § 2-207(2) asks whether both parties are (§ 2-104(3)). For §§ 2-201(2), 2-205, 2-207 and 2-209, which rest on ordinary business practices, almost every person in business is a merchant, but a lawyer buying fishing tackle for personal use is not (§ 2-104 cmt. 2). new.label: Who offered, the vendor or the buyer?
new.detail: Decide who offered and when the deal was complete (see K-10). Under Hill, the vendor’s terms in the box are part of its offer, the buyer accepts by keeping the goods past the return period, and with only one form § 2-207 is irrelevant. Under Klocek, the buyer offered, the box terms are an acceptance or confirmation proposing additional terms, and § 2-207 applies to the single form.
